title: Chapter 19 — The Prophet
paragraphs: "Shipmates, have you signed on to that ship?"

Queequeg and I had just left the Pequod and were strolling away from the water, each lost in his own thoughts, when a stranger spoke these words to us. Pausing in front of us, he aimed his heavy forefinger at the ship in question. He was shabbily dressed in a faded jacket and patched trousers, with a rag of a black handkerchief around his neck. A severe case of smallpox had flowed across his face in every direction and left it like the scarred, ribbed bed of a dried-up stream.
"Have you signed on to her?" he repeated.
"You mean the ship Pequod, I suppose," said I, trying to buy a little more time for a good look at him.
"Yes, the Pequod — that ship there," he said, pulling his whole arm back and then thrusting it straight out, his pointed finger aimed like a bayonet at the vessel.
"Yes," said I, "we've just signed the articles."
"Anything in there about your souls?"
"About what?"

"Oh, maybe you haven't got any," he said quickly. "No matter though. I know plenty of fellows who haven't got any — good luck to them. They're all the better off for it. A soul is a sort of fifth wheel on a wagon."
"What are you going on about, shipmate?" said I.
"He's got enough soul, though, to make up for what's missing in other men," the stranger said abruptly, placing a nervous emphasis on the word he.
"Queequeg," said I, "let's go. This fellow has escaped from somewhere. He's talking about something and somebody we don't know."
"Stop!" cried the stranger. "You spoke true — you haven't seen Old Thunder yet, have you?"
"Who's Old Thunder?" said I, caught again by the unsettling intensity of his manner.
"Captain Ahab."
"What! The captain of our ship, the Pequod?"
"Yes, some of us old sailor types call him that. You haven't seen him yet, have you?"
"No, we haven't. They say he's sick, but getting better, and he'll be fine again before long."
"Fine again before long!" the stranger laughed — a solemn, mocking kind of laugh. "Listen: when Captain Ahab is fine, then this left arm of mine will be fine. Not before."
"What do you know about him?"
"What did they tell you about him? Tell me that!"
"They didn't say much of anything about him. I've only heard he's a good whale-hunter and a good captain to his crew."

"That's true — both true enough. But you'd better jump when he gives an order. Obey and complain — complain and obey — that's how it works with Captain Ahab. But nothing about what happened to him off Cape Horn, long ago, when he lay like a dead man for three days and nights? Nothing about that deadly fight with the Spaniard in front of the altar in Santa? Heard nothing about that, eh? Nothing about the silver cup he spat into? And nothing about losing his leg last voyage, just as was prophesied? Didn't you hear a word about any of that and more? No, I don't think you did — how could you? Who knows about it? Not all of Nantucket, I expect. But anyhow, maybe you've heard about the leg and how he lost it. Yes, you have heard about that, I'm sure. Oh yes, that everyone knows — almost. I mean they know he's got only one leg, and that a sperm whale took the other."

"My friend," said I, "I have no idea what all this rambling of yours is about, and I don't much care. It seems to me you must be a little damaged in the head. But if you're talking about Captain Ahab of that ship there, the Pequod, then let me tell you — I know all about the loss of his leg."
"All about it, eh? Sure you do? All?"
"Pretty sure."

With finger pointed and eye fixed on the Pequod, the beggar-like stranger stood a moment, as if in a troubled daydream. Then, starting slightly, he turned and said: "So you've signed on, have you? Names down on the papers? Well, well, what's signed is signed. And what's to be will be — and then again, maybe it won't be after all. Anyway, it's all fixed and arranged already. Some sailors or other have to go with him, I suppose — might as well be you as anyone. God pity them! Good morning to you, shipmates, morning. The heavens bless you. I'm sorry I stopped you."
"Look here, friend," said I, "if you have something important to tell us, out with it. But if you're just trying to trick us, you've picked the wrong men. That's all I have to say."

"And well said — I like hearing a man speak up like that. You're just the right sort for him — exactly the type. Good morning, shipmates, morning! Oh! And when you get there, tell them I've decided not to be one of the crew."
"Ah, my friend, you can't fool us that way — you can't fool us. It's the easiest thing in the world for a man to act as though he carries a great secret."
"Good morning, shipmates, morning."
"Morning it is," said I. "Come along, Queequeg, let's leave this crazy man. But stop — tell me your name, will you?"
"Elijah."

Elijah! I thought. And we walked away, both commenting in our own way on this ragged old sailor, and agreed he was nothing but a fraud trying to scare us. But we hadn't gone a hundred yards when, turning a corner and glancing back, who should I see but Elijah following us at a distance. The sight struck me so forcefully that I said nothing to Queequeg about it. I just walked on with my companion, wanting to see if the stranger would turn the same corner we did. He did. And then it seemed he was following us, though for what purpose I couldn't imagine. This, combined with his vague, half-hinting, half-revealing way of talking, stirred up all kinds of shadowy suspicions in me — all connected with the Pequod, and Captain Ahab, and his lost leg, and the Cape Horn incident, and the silver cup, and what Captain Peleg had said about him the day before, and the prediction of the old woman Tistig, and the voyage we had committed ourselves to, and a hundred other dark things.

I decided to find out for certain whether this ragged Elijah was truly following us. Queequeg and I crossed to the other side of the street and retraced our steps. But Elijah walked straight past without seeming to notice us. This was a relief, and once more — and finally, as it seemed to me — I decided in my heart that he was nothing but a fraud.
